subtitle: SoD Conflict Testing
intro: Pull the current Segregation of Duties (SoD) conflict report for Accounts Payable and confirm whether vendor master maintenance and payment run execution sit on the same user ID.

exec_table.directions: In GRC Access Risk Analysis, select the risk ID for "create/change vendor master + execute payment run" (typically a P2P-ruleset risk) and run at the user level for the Accounts Payable organizational unit. [Navigation: from the Fiori Launchpad, open the 'Access Risk Analysis' tile (use the App Finder search if it isn't pinned to your home page) — or in NWBC, expand GRC → Access Management → Access Risk Analysis in the left-hand menu. Set Analysis Type = User Level, use the risk field's value-help to select the P2P vendor-master/payment-run risk ID, restrict the Organizational Unit filter to Accounts Payable, then click Search/Execute to run the analysis.]

Export the results list — this is your population of flagged users. [Navigation: with the results list open, click the Export icon (spreadsheet/download icon, top-right of the results toolbar) and choose Excel as the format; save using your evidence file naming convention.]

For each flagged user, use PFCG in display mode to confirm which role(s) actually carry both authorization objects (F_LFA1_BUK combined with F110-related objects). [Navigation: type PFCG in the SAP GUI command field (top left) and press Enter. Enter the role name in the Role field and click the Display icon (glasses) — never the Change (pencil) icon. Open the Authorizations tab, click 'Display Authorization Data' to expand the tree, and locate F_LFA1_BUK and the F110 authorization objects.]

Cross-check against SUIM → Users by Complex Selection Criteria to confirm the user's role assignment history, in case a role was recently changed. [You can also confirm role-to-user assignment directly via SE16N on tables USR02 / AGR_USERS as of a specific date.] [Navigation: type SUIM in the command field and press Enter; in the tree expand Users → By Complex Selection Criteria, enter the user ID, and press F8 to execute.]

If a mitigating control is claimed, request the GRC Mitigation ID and pull its documentation from the GRC Rule Book / Mitigation Assignment screen. [Navigation: from the GRC Fiori Launchpad or NWBC, open the Rule Book / Mitigation Assignment app, enter the Mitigation ID in the search field, and open the resulting record to screenshot the control description and last review date.]

evidence: A dated export of the Access Risk Analysis report, the specific role names and authorization objects in conflict, and (if applicable) the mitigating control ID with its last review date.
pitfall: Running Access Risk Analysis at the role level instead of the user level can hide a real conflict if two separate, individually-clean roles combine to create a conflict only when assigned together to the same person. Always confirm at the user level.

subtitle: New-Hire & Turnover Access Testing
intro: Confirm a newly provisioned user was assigned the correct, current role — not a legacy or deactivated role template — following a personnel change.

exec_table.directions: Pull the HR termination/new-hire report for the test period from HR (outside SAP) and cross-reference names against SU01 active user records. [SUIM's RSUSR200 report — users by logon date/lock status — is a useful cross-check here too.] [Navigation: type SU01 in the command field and press Enter, enter the user ID, and click Display; check the Logon Data tab for lock status and the Roles tab for assigned roles and validity dates.]

For each new hire in the sample, open the GRC Access Request History and confirm the requested role matches the intended, current role design (not an old composite role). [Navigation: from the GRC Fiori Launchpad, open 'My Access Requests' or 'Access Request History', filter by requestor/date, and open the specific request to view the approval trail.]

Use PFCG in display mode to confirm the assigned role's authorization objects match what the current process design calls for. [Navigation: type PFCG in the command field, press Enter, enter the role name, click Display, and review the Authorizations tab.]
Document any mismatch between what was requested, what was approved, and what was actually provisioned.

evidence: The access request workflow printout/export showing requestor, approver, and role granted; a screenshot of SU01 showing the role assignment and validity date.

subtitle: SoD Testing Outside Finance (Procurement)
intro: Run the same SoD methodology used for Accounts Payable against a different process area — Procurement — where the risk pairing is different (vendor master create + PO approval, rather than vendor master + payment run).

exec_table.directions: Run Access Risk Analysis scoped specifically to the Procurement process area — do not assume the AP ruleset automatically covers Procurement; confirm the correct risk IDs are in scope. [Navigation: from the Fiori Launchpad, open 'Access Risk Analysis', switch the ruleset/process area filter to Procurement, select the ME21N + XK01/XK02 risk ID(s), and click Search/Execute.]

For any newly flagged conflict, check SUIM's transaction usage history to determine whether the access has actually been used, which affects severity but not the underlying finding. [SE16N on tables EKKO/EKPO can also confirm the user's actual PO activity.] [Navigation: type SUIM in the command field, press Enter, then open Users → By Transaction Executed (or type ST03N directly) to pull usage history for the flagged user.]
Interview the business process owner (BPO) using the same posture the story models — explain what the access allows, not what has happened.
Document the population of similarly structured roles across other non-finance departments before closing the finding, since a gap found in one area often repeats in others.

evidence: The Procurement-scoped risk analysis export, SUIM transaction usage history for the flagged user, and a summary memo documenting the BPO conversation.

subtitle: Fiori Launchpad Security Testing
intro: Confirm that a Fiori launchpad tile's front-end catalog/group assignment does not grant visibility beyond what the user's backend role actually authorizes.

exec_table.directions: In /UI2/FLPD_CUST or Manage Launchpad Pages, identify every tile visible to the test user's assigned business catalog(s). [Navigation: type /UI2/FLPD_CUST in the command field and press Enter (or open the 'Manage Launchpad Pages' Fiori tile). Select the business catalog assigned to the test user and expand it to list every tile/target mapping it contains.]
For each tile touching a sensitive function (payment, vendor master, journal posting), note the underlying OData service or target mapping (Fiori app → semantic object/action).

Cross-reference that OData service in SU24 to identify which authorization objects the backend actually checks. [Navigation: type SU24 in the command field, press Enter, enter the transaction code or OData service name, and press Enter/F8 to display the check indicator table.]

Compare against PFCG for the user's assigned backend role — confirm every authorization object the tile could reach is genuinely restricted, not just assumed restricted because "the tile isn't supposed to be there." [Navigation: type PFCG in the command field, press Enter, enter the role, click Display, and open the Authorizations tab to compare object values.]
Log into a test user session (or use "Run As" if your GRC configuration supports it) and attempt the transaction through the tile directly to confirm where, exactly, the block occurs.

evidence: Screenshots of the visible tile, the SU24 check indicator table for the relevant service, and the PFCG authorization object values for the assigned role, with the specific screen where access was ultimately blocked (or not).
pitfall: A tile that is merely invisible to a role does not mean the underlying service is protected — test the actual OData call or transaction directly, not just what appears on the launchpad.

subtitle: Emergency Access Management (EAM) Testing
intro: Confirm every firefighter (emergency access) ID activation for the period has a completed, independent log review on file.

exec_table.directions: In the Firefighter Log Report app, pull all firefighter ID activations for the test period. [Navigation: from the GRC Fiori Launchpad, open the 'Firefighter Log Report' tile, set the date range to the test period, and click Go/Search.]
For each activation, confirm a review status of "Reviewed" or "Approved" with a reviewer name and date populated — not blank or defaulted.

For any activation without a completed review, pull the underlying transaction log via SM20 for that user ID and time window to reconstruct what was actually done. [Navigation: type SM20 in the command field, press Enter, enter the firefighter user ID and date/time window, and press F8 to execute.]

Compare the stated business justification on the activation request against the transactions actually executed in SM20 to confirm reasonableness. [The justification text is captured in GRAC_SPM at activation time.] [Navigation: GRAC_SPM is reached from the GRC Fiori Launchpad ('Firefighter Login'/'Firefighter Log Report' tiles) rather than direct SAP GUI entry in most configurations; open the specific activation record to view the justification text.]

evidence: The full-period Firefighter Log Report export, with review status per line, plus SM20 transaction detail for any unreviewed activation.
pitfall: Firefighter activation and firefighter log review are two separate steps in GRC — confirm you are testing the review completion field specifically, not just that the ID was properly assigned and activated.

subtitle: Joiner-Mover-Leaver (Termination Access) Testing
intro: Confirm that every terminated employee's SAP access was deactivated on or before their last working day, with no login activity afterward.

exec_table.directions: Obtain the HR termination list for the test period (outside SAP). [Also check the most recent User Access Review recertification cycle to confirm whether this person should have already been flagged there.]

For each terminated employee, run SU01 to confirm the account is locked and/or the validity end date is on or before the termination date. [Navigation: type SU01 in the command field, press Enter, enter the user ID, click Display, and check the Logon Data tab (lock status) and Address/Roles tabs (validity dates).]

Run SUIM RSUSR200 for the full population, sorted by last logon date, to catch anyone with SAP activity after their stated termination date. [Navigation: type SUIM in the command field, press Enter, expand Users → By Complex Selection Criteria (or type RSUSR200 directly), set the selection criteria, press F8, then sort the results by Last Logon Date.]

For any post-termination login found, pull SM20 for that user ID and time window to document exactly what was accessed. [Navigation: type SM20 in the command field, press Enter, enter the user ID and date/time window, and press F8 (Execute) to display the log.]
Trace the deprovisioning request itself back to its source — was it submitted, and if so, was it submitted late? This tells you whether the gap is a process-timing issue or a process-existence issue.

evidence: The HR termination list, the SU01 lock-status screenshot for each tested user, the RSUSR200 report, and SM20 detail for any exception.

subtitle: Change Management Testing
intro: Confirm every production transport moved with a corresponding CAB approval (standard) or completed emergency justification form (emergency path) within the required window.

exec_table.directions: In STMS, pull the import history for the production system for the test period — this is your population of all transports moved. [SE03 can also search transports by date range, developer, or object type across the full landscape.] [Navigation: type STMS in the command field and press Enter, click the Import Overview icon, select the production system's queue, and filter by date to pull the import history for the test period.]

For each transport number, use SE01 to confirm the transport's description, contents (programs, config tables touched), and release timestamp. [Navigation: type SE01 in the command field, press Enter, enter the transport request number, and click Display to view its description, object list, and release timestamp.]
Cross-reference each transport number against the change ticket system to confirm a matching, approved CAB ticket exists.

For any transport without a matching standard ticket, check whether it was logged as an emergency change; confirm the emergency justification form was completed within the required window (e.g., 48 hours) of the transport's import timestamp.
Flag and log, with exact transport numbers and timestamps, any transport with neither a standard ticket nor a completed emergency form.

evidence: The STMS import history export (with timestamps), the SE01 transport detail for each sampled transport, and the matched (or unmatched) change ticket reference.
pitfall: STMS shows when a transport was imported, not when it was released from development — use SE01's release timestamp, not the import timestamp, when testing against an approval that should have preceded the transport's creation.

subtitle: Change Management at Scale
intro: Apply the same transport-to-approval testing methodology as Book 2, but across a high-volume system upgrade/cutover event, confirming the process held under real volume.

exec_table.directions: Scope your population to the exact cutover window (e.g., a specific Friday 6 p.m. to Sunday midnight). [Depending on what the cutover included, you may also need to review patch-level changes via SPAM/SAINT and any client refresh/copy activity via SCC3.]

Pull the complete transport list for that window via SE03, across every system in the landscape that was part of the cutover. [Navigation: type SE03 in the command field and press Enter, choose 'Transports by Date and Time' (or similar search), enter the cutover window's start and end date/time, and execute.]
Sample a statistically appropriate subset (not just a handful) given the elevated volume — this event is exactly the kind of high-risk window that warrants a larger sample than a routine month.

For each sampled transport, confirm standard or emergency approval exactly as in Book 2's methodology, paying particular attention to timestamps near the edges of the emergency-approval window under real time pressure. [Navigation: type STMS in the command field, press Enter, and check the import queue/history for each sampled system for approval evidence exactly as in Book 2.]

evidence: The full cutover-window transport population, your sample selection methodology and rationale (documented, given the elevated volume), and approval evidence for each sampled item.

subtitle: Vendor-Executed Change Testing
intro: Confirm that changes executed by an outsourced/managed-services vendor carry the same evidentiary trail as internally executed changes, per the contractually required format.

exec_table.directions: Pull the transport population for the period exactly as in Book 2, filtering to transports executed under the vendor's designated service account(s). [Navigation: type STMS in the command field, press Enter, and pull the import history, filtering the transport list by the vendor's service account in the 'exported by' or requestor column.]
Request the vendor's own change log export for the same period and period-match it against the SAP transport log.
Confirm every vendor-executed emergency change has a completed justification form within the contractually required window, in the format your own reconciliation bridge requires.

Independently sample-test a subset of the vendor's self-reported log against Thornfield's own SAP system logs (STMS/SM20) rather than accepting the vendor's report at face value. [Navigation: type SU01 (or SUIM's user list) in the command field, press Enter, and independently pull system logs via STMS/SM20 for cross-checking rather than relying on the vendor's export.]

evidence: The vendor's change log export, the independent SAP-side transport log used to verify it, and documentation of any variance between the two.
pitfall: Never accept a vendor's self-reported completion log as sufficient evidence on its own — independently reconcile it against your own system's transport and system logs.

subtitle: Computer Operations Testing
intro: Confirm that a sample backup can actually be restored, not merely that the nightly backup job reports "Success."

exec_table.directions: Pull the full population of nightly backup completion reports for the test period via DB13/DB12 — confirm every night shows "Success." [Navigation: type DB13 in the command field and press Enter to view the DBA Planning Calendar; double-click a completed backup job, or type DB12 directly, to open its detailed completion log.]
Do not stop there: request that Basis perform a live restoration of a recent backup to an isolated, non-production environment.
Observe (or request evidence of) the actual restore process, including elapsed time and any errors encountered.

Once restored, confirm the recovered environment is usable — log in, run a basic report, and confirm data matches production as of the backup date. [Navigation: type ST04 in the command field and press Enter to review the restored instance's database performance/administration overview once Basis completes the test restore.]
Document the full restoration procedure as evidence the control is real, not just scheduled.

evidence: The DB13/DB12 completion log population, plus a documented, evidenced record of an actual test restoration — elapsed time, any errors found and corrected, and confirmation the restored data was usable.
pitfall: A green "Success" status in DB13 only confirms the backup job completed without an error code. It says nothing about whether the resulting file is actually restorable — that has to be tested directly, at least annually.

subtitle: Interface Control Testing
intro: Confirm that records passing between SAP and a third-party or legacy system are not silently dropped by checking the interface's own error/failure log, not just its completion status.

exec_table.directions: Identify the interface's technology (IDoc, RFC, or PI/PO) and pull the corresponding monitor (WE02, SM58, or SXMB_MONI) for the test period. [Navigation: for IDocs, type WE02 (or WE05) in the command field, press Enter, and enter the message type and date range; for RFC-based interfaces type SM58 and press Enter; for PI/PO interfaces type SXMB_MONI and press Enter. Press F8/Execute to display the monitor.]
Reconcile total record volume sent by the source system against total records successfully posted in SAP for the same period — do not just confirm the batch job "completed."

For any variance, drill into the error/failure log specifically (not just the success count) to identify individual failed records and their error reason. [Navigation: type BD87 in the command field, press Enter, and filter for IDocs in error status within the test period to drill into individual failure reasons.]

Cross-reference a sample of failed records against the source system to confirm whether the underlying business transaction (e.g., a physical inventory receipt) still exists and was simply never reflected in SAP.

evidence: The source-system record count, the SAP-side received/posted count, the interface error log detail for any variance, and the physical/source-system confirmation for a sample of dropped records.
pitfall: A batch job reporting "complete" only confirms the job ran end to end — it does not confirm every individual record inside the batch was successfully processed. Always check the record-level error log, not just the job-level status.

subtitle: Custom Code / ABAP Security Testing
intro: Confirm that a custom (Z/Y-prefixed) transaction enforces the same authorization checks as the standard transaction it was built to shortcut.

exec_table.directions: Pull the full inventory of custom (Z/Y) transactions in the landscape via SE93 search by namespace. [Navigation: type SE93 in the command field, press Enter, and search by the Z/Y namespace prefix (or use the transaction search in SE16N on table TSTC) to inventory custom transactions.]

For each transaction touching a sensitive process (vendor master, payments, journal entries), open the linked program in SE38/SE80 (display mode) and review its AUTHORITY-CHECK statements. [Navigation: type SE38 (or SE80) in the command field, press Enter, enter the program name, and click Display (not Change/Edit) to review the source code and locate AUTHORITY-CHECK statements.]

Compare the authorization objects and values actually checked in the custom program against SU24's standard default values for the equivalent standard transaction. [Navigation: type SU24 in the command field, press Enter, enter the equivalent standard transaction code, and press Enter/F8 to display its default authorization object values.]

Where the custom program's check is narrower, missing, or independently written rather than referencing the same objects, test directly with a restricted test user to confirm whether the restriction actually holds.

Run SCI (Code Inspector) across the full custom code population to identify other transactions with the same pattern, rather than stopping at the one instance found. [Navigation: type SCI in the command field, press Enter, select or create a variant scoping the custom code population, and execute the check.]

evidence: The SE93 transaction definition, the relevant AUTHORITY-CHECK code excerpt, the SU24 comparison, and a live test confirming whether a restricted user could or could not bypass the standard control through the custom transaction.
pitfall: Reading the code is necessary but not sufficient — always confirm the finding with an actual test using a real, restricted test user ID, since authorization logic can behave differently than the code appears to suggest.

subtitle: Manual Journal Entry Review Testing
intro: Confirm every journal entry above the review threshold carries a documented, independent secondary approval, and identify whether the workflow's routing threshold is correctly configured.

exec_table.directions: Pull the full population of journal entries above the stated review threshold for the test period via FBL3N, filtered by document type and amount. [Navigation: type FBL3N in the command field, press Enter, set the document type and amount filters on the selection screen, and press F8 to execute.]

For each sampled entry, use FB03 to open the document and check the workflow/release strategy tab for a completed approval, or a null result. [Navigation: type FB03 in the command field, press Enter, enter the document number, and press Enter to display it; check the workflow/release strategy tab or status field.]

Where a workflow exists, use SWI1/SWIA to confirm the specific work item was completed by an approver independent of the preparer, with a timestamp. [Navigation: type SWI1 (or SWIA) in the command field, press Enter, filter by the work item/document reference, and press F8 to display completion status and timestamp.]

Separately, confirm the underlying workflow threshold configuration itself (via SPRO or the relevant config table, display mode only) matches the documented policy threshold — do not assume the two are the same without checking. [Navigation: type SPRO in the command field, press Enter, and drill into the relevant IMG node for the release strategy/workflow threshold — display only, do not change; alternatively query the configuration table directly in SE16N.]

For any entry above the threshold with no completed approval, escalate immediately rather than waiting to complete the full sample — this pattern (as in the story) often points to a configuration issue affecting many entries, not just one.

evidence: The FBL3N population export, FB03 screenshots showing approval status per sampled entry, SWI1 workflow completion detail, and the confirmed configuration threshold value.
pitfall: Do not test only the entries the report shows as "above threshold" — independently recompute the population directly from FBL3N, since a misconfigured threshold (as in the story) will cause the workflow's own report to under-report exactly the entries you're looking for.

subtitle: Acquired-Entity Controls Assessment
intro: Assess whether an acquired entity's manual journal entry review control is genuinely system-enforced or exists only as an unenforced policy, and confirm the interim compensating control's evidence trail.

exec_table.directions: Confirm, in writing, whether the acquired entity's stated review control is enforced by any system mechanism at all, or is entirely dependent on an individual's manual review. [Navigation: if configuration has begun, type SPRO in the command field, press Enter, and review the relevant workflow IMG node in display mode.]
If manual, request the full population of the compensating control's evidence (e.g., monthly reviewer sign-off emails) for the full period since acquisition — not a pre-selected sample.

Test a sample of underlying entries against that evidence to confirm the review actually happened as documented, not just that a log exists. [Navigation: type FB03 or FBL3N in the command field, press Enter, and pull the entity's postings exactly as in standard R2R testing if migrated to SAP; if not yet migrated, request the equivalent extract from the legacy system.]
Document the root-cause gap (no system enforcement) as a distinct finding from any individual exceptions found in testing the entries themselves.

evidence: The full population of manual review evidence, your sample testing results against that population, and a written root-cause description of the system-enforcement gap.

subtitle: Investigating a Specific Journal Entry
intro: Reconstruct the full history and underlying support for a specific journal entry flagged by an anonymous tip, independent of the original tester's prior conclusion.

exec_table.directions: Do not start from the original workpaper's conclusion — reconstruct the population independently via FBL3N or SE16N directly against BKPF/BSEG. [Navigation: type FBL3N in the command field, press Enter, and re-run the population query with your own selection criteria; alternatively type SE16N, press Enter, enter table BKPF or BSEG, and press F8 to query directly.]

For the specific entry in question, use FB03's document change history to determine whether it was altered after initial posting. [Navigation: with the document open in FB03, go to Environment → Document Changes in the top menu, and press Enter/Execute to display the change history log.]

Independently obtain the underlying support (e.g., the actuarial claims data referenced in a reserve estimate) directly from its source system or owner, rather than accepting a prepared summary at face value.
Recompute the estimate or calculation independently where possible, and compare your independent result against what was actually booked.
Document every step of the reconstruction, since this file may ultimately be reviewed by Internal Audit, External Audit, or Legal.

evidence: The independently re-pulled population, the FB03 change history, the source-system support obtained directly (not via a prepared summary), and your independent recomputation.
pitfall: When investigating a tip that touches a previously tested item, always rebuild the population and pull support independently rather than reusing the original workpaper's extract — the whole point of the investigation is to test whether the original evidence chain itself can be trusted.

subtitle: GRC Process Control (CCM) Testing
intro: Confirm an automated business rule inside GRC Process Control is not merely scheduled and "running," but is actually evaluating current data correctly.

exec_table.directions: Pull the automated rule's historical exception output for a meaningful trailing period (at least six to eight cycles), not just the most recent run.
Look specifically for an exception rate that has dropped to zero, or is otherwise inconsistent with historical baseline, which is your indicator of a possible silent failure.

Use SM37 to confirm the underlying background job is genuinely executing without technical errors — this rules out a simple scheduling failure and points you toward a logic/configuration issue instead. [Navigation: type SM37 in the command field, press Enter, set the job name/user and date range, and press F8 to display the job log and status.]

Independently query the source table(s) via SE16N to manually identify what the rule should have flagged, and compare that against what the rule actually reported. [Navigation: type SE16N in the command field, press Enter, enter the source table name, set your selection criteria, and press F8 to query.]

If a mismatch is found, trace the rule's configuration (reference tables, thresholds, field mappings) to identify the specific root cause. [This configuration lives in the Business Rules / Automated Monitoring app.]

evidence: The rule's historical exception-count trend, the SM37 job execution log, your independent SE16N-based recomputation of what should have been flagged, and the root-cause configuration detail.
pitfall: A background job showing "completed successfully" in SM37 only confirms the job ran — it says nothing about whether the rule's underlying logic is still correctly evaluating current data. Always independently test the output against a manual recomputation.

subtitle: GRC Risk Management Testing
intro: Confirm every risk marked "mitigated" in the enterprise risk register actually references a real, currently active, tested control.

exec_table.directions: Export the full risk register, including every risk's stated mitigation status and linked control reference ID. [Navigation: from the GRC Fiori Launchpad or NWBC, open the Risk Register / Risk Workbench app, and use the export icon in the toolbar to download the full register.]
Independently cross-reference every control ID against the current, active control inventory — do not assume a listed reference is valid without checking.

For any control reference that does not resolve to a real, current control, document it as a broken link and determine whether a real control exists under a different name/reference, or whether no control actually exists at all. [Navigation: type SE16N in the command field, press Enter, enter the relevant control/config table, and press F8 to confirm whether the referenced control object still exists.]
For confirmed gaps, assess the underlying risk directly and determine whether new remediation work is required, distinct from simply correcting the register's documentation.

evidence: The full risk register export, your control-reference cross-reference results, and documentation of any risk requiring new remediation as a result.
pitfall: The risk register is a claim about evidence, not evidence itself — never conclude a risk is mitigated because the register says so without independently confirming the referenced control actually exists and is current.

subtitle: Supporting Executive & Board Reporting
intro: As a junior consultant, your role is to ensure every deficiency in your own testing population is completely and accurately reflected in the underlying tracker your Senior Lead uses to brief the Compliance Director and, ultimately, the CFO.

exec_table.directions: Before any status reporting deadline, confirm every finding you personally identified is logged in the tracker with the same specificity you would want if you were the one explaining it to the CFO. [Navigation: from the GRC Fiori Launchpad, open the Issue / Deficiency Tracker app and confirm each finding you identified has a complete entry — description, root cause, and status.]
Never let a finding exist only in your own notes or a side conversation — the written tracker entry is what eventually becomes a sentence in a board deck.
If asked to summarize your own testing status, report the honest state — including anything still open or uncertain — rather than rounding up to sound more complete than it is.

evidence: A tracker entry, for every finding, dated the day it was identified, in your own words, before anyone has decided what to do about it.

subtitle: Supporting an SEC Response
intro: As a junior consultant, your role in an SEC comment letter response is to accurately assemble and organize the underlying evidence file — not to draft the legal response itself.

exec_table.directions: When asked to assemble evidence for a regulatory response, pull the complete, unedited population for the full period in question — never a curated subset. [Navigation: use FB03, FBL3N, or SE16N as applicable — type the transaction in the command field, press Enter, and re-pull the complete population for the full period without pre-filtering to a subset.]
Organize your evidence file exactly the way it will be presented: by month, by control, with clear labeling, so your Senior Lead and Legal can move quickly under a hard deadline.
Flag any gaps in the evidence honestly and immediately — a missing month of documentation found on day two of a ten-day response window is a manageable problem; found on day nine, it is not.

evidence: The complete, organized evidence population for the period in question, with any gaps flagged in writing the moment they're found.

subtitle: Supporting a Disclosure Controls Review
intro: Recognize when a finding from your own routine testing might carry disclosure implications outside standard ICFR testing, and escalate immediately rather than treating it as a routine finding.

exec_table.directions: If routine testing surfaces a reference to a security incident, system outage, or similar event with no clear record of legal/disclosure evaluation, do not simply note it and move on. [If the finding involves an emergency system change, cross-reference the transport log via STMS/SE01 as well.] [Navigation: type SM21 (System Log) or SM20 (Security Audit Log) in the command field, press Enter, set the date/time window, and press F8 to display entries around the event.]
Escalate to your Senior Lead the same day, with the specific reference (ticket number, transport number, date) that led you to notice it.
Do not attempt to assess materiality or disclosure requirements yourself — that determination belongs to Legal and your Senior Lead; your job is accurate, fast escalation of what you found.

evidence: The specific system reference (ticket, transport, or log entry) that surfaced the gap, and a dated record of when you escalated it.

subtitle: Data Privacy / Retention Testing
intro: Confirm that personal data (former employee or vendor contact records) is not retained in the live system beyond its stated retention policy limit.

exec_table.directions: Confirm the written retention policy's specific time limit (e.g., three years post-termination) and the categories of data it covers.

Use SE16N to pull the full population of relevant records (e.g., all terminated employees, or all inactive vendor contacts) with their relevant date fields. [SUIM or the S_ALR_* standard reports can also identify inactive/terminated records by date.] [Navigation: type SE16N in the command field, press Enter, enter table PA0002 (or the relevant vendor master table), add the relevant date field to the selection screen, and press F8.]

Filter for any record exceeding the policy's stated retention window that has not been anonymized, archived, or purged. [Navigation: from the same SE16N result list, use the filter icon on the date column to isolate records older than the retention window.]

Confirm whether any technical enforcement mechanism exists at all (ILM configuration, a scheduled job, or similar) versus the policy existing only as a document with no system-side enforcement. [Navigation: type IRM_CUST or ILM_SIL in the command field, press Enter, and review the configured retention rules in display mode.]

evidence: The full population export with age calculations, and documentation of whether a technical enforcement mechanism exists.
pitfall: A written retention policy is not evidence of a control — confirm there is an actual, scheduled, system-side mechanism enforcing it before concluding the control operates effectively.

subtitle: SAP Licensing Exposure Testing
intro: Identify transaction volume flowing into SAP from third-party or self-service systems under a generic/service user ID, and confirm whether that access pattern has been evaluated for licensing implications.

exec_table.directions: Use SM59 to inventory every active RFC connection between SAP and an external/third-party system. [Navigation: type SM59 in the command field, press Enter, and expand each connection type (ABAP, HTTP, TCP/IP) to inventory active RFC destinations.]

For each connection, use ST03N and SE16N to quantify the actual transaction volume and type flowing through that connection over a representative period. [Navigation: type ST03N in the command field, press Enter, and drill into workload statistics by user/RFC connection for the representative period; type SE16N separately to query relevant transaction tables like VBAK for volume by user ID.]

Run USMM to review how the system currently classifies this usage for licensing purposes, and compare that classification against the actual technical access pattern you've documented. [Navigation: type USMM in the command field, press Enter, and press F8/Execute to run the system measurement; review the user classification and engine-based metrics tabs.]

Escalate any material, unquantified indirect access pattern to your Senior Lead for a formal licensing exposure assessment — this determination requires input from IT, Legal, and often outside licensing counsel, not a conclusion you would reach alone.

evidence: The full RFC connection inventory, transaction volume analysis per connection, and the current USMM classification for comparison.
pitfall: This same RFC/service-account analysis is exactly how you would test any generic or shared account for excessive, unmonitored access — not just for licensing exposure. If a shared account exists for convenience, the volume-and-classification method here is the test, regardless of which risk prompted it.

subtitle: Two-Way vs. Three-Way Match Configuration Testing
intro: Confirm whether the three-way match (purchase order, goods receipt, invoice) is actually configured and enforced at every plant, not just documented in the control matrix.

exec_table.directions: Display table EKPO (purchase order line items) with fields WEPOS (goods receipt indicator) and REPOS (invoice receipt indicator) added via field selection — they are not on the default layout. Filter WEPOS blank to find lines configured for two-way match with no goods receipt expected. Add WERKS (plant) and re-run, since match configuration is set per plant, not company-wide. [Navigation: type SE16N in the command field, enter EKPO, use Change Field Selection to add WEPOS/REPOS to the display, set your date range, execute, then re-run grouped by WERKS.]

Pull the transport/change history for the two-way-match configuration to establish when it moved to production. [Navigation: type SE01 or STMS in the command field and review the change/transport log for the relevant configuration table.]
Display table RSEG (invoice line items) for your test period and select a sample with PO references. [Navigation: type SE16N, enter RSEG, set your date range, execute.]

Display the purchase order for each sampled invoice and open the Purchase Order History tab — confirm all three documents exist and check the posting order. [Navigation: type ME23N, enter the PO number, open the Purchase Order History tab.]
Pull the material document list as an independent check that the goods receipt is real. [Navigation: type MB51, enter the material/plant and date range, execute.]

evidence: The EKPO extract by plant showing which plants are configured for two-way match, the transport/change history for that configuration, and at least one ME23N Purchase Order History screenshot showing the posting-date sequence of PO, goods receipt, and invoice.
pitfall: A clean sample proves nothing if the underlying configuration only ever allows a match to occur — test the configuration itself before testing transactions against it, since a setting that cannot fail is not a control.

subtitle: Payment Run Duplicate & SoD Testing
intro: Test whether the payment run process can produce — and would catch — a duplicate bank file transmission, and confirm proposal creation and release are performed by different people.

exec_table.directions: Open the payment run screen for your period. Touch nothing that executes — this screen moves money. [Navigation: type F110 in the command field, open Edit → Proposal → Proposal list or the payment run log, and set your period.]

Record four things per run: run date/ID, who created the proposal, who released it, and the total value. Compare creator and releaser — a match is a segregation-of-duties failure on the company's largest single money movement.
Display tables REGUH (payment run header) and REGUP (line items) to get the population independent of the F110 screen. [Navigation: type SE16N, enter REGUH or REGUP, set your date range, execute.]

Check how many transmission records each payment file has — one is correct, more than one means the file was sent twice. [Navigation: type FDTA in the command field, or review the DMEE tree for the relevant payment medium format.]
Check the transmission job log — a re-run is visible here as a second execution of the same job. [Navigation: type SM37, enter the job name and date range, execute.]

evidence: The payment run list showing proposal creator and run executor side by side, the count of runs where those two names match, and the transmission record count per file from FDTA/DMEE.
pitfall: The population is the payment run log, not the list of approved proposals — a run executed without ever going through the approved-proposal list will not appear there, so starting from the approved list will understate what actually happened.

subtitle: Vendor Bank Detail Change Testing
intro: Confirm that changes to a vendor's bank details are independently approved before the next payment, for every company code — not just the ones covered when workflow was first configured.

exec_table.directions: Display table CDHDR for the vendor/business partner object class over your date range — this tells you a change happened, not what changed. [Navigation: type SE16N, enter CDHDR, set your date range, execute.]

Display table CDPOS for field-level detail. Filter on bank-related field names and record field, old value, new value, user, and date/time. [Navigation: type SE16N, enter CDPOS, filter on the bank fields, execute.]
Cross-check one vendor via change display as a readable confirmation of the CDPOS extract. [Navigation: type FK04 or BP, enter the vendor, open change display.]
Check the workflow log for each change — confirm an approval exists and that the approver is not the requester. [Navigation: type SWI1, filter by object type and date, review the approval trail.]
For each bank-detail change, find the next payment to that vendor and measure the gap in days. [Navigation: via SE16N table REGUP, filter by vendor and date after the change date.]

evidence: The CDPOS extract of bank-field changes with old/new values, the corresponding workflow approval status for each, and the day-count from each change to the next payment to that vendor.
pitfall: This needs no privileged access, only the ability to edit a master record — and the population must come from the change documents, not the workflow log, since a change that never routed for approval will not appear in the log at all. The same CDHDR/CDPOS technique tests any master-data field an auditor cares about — pricing conditions, payment terms, tax classification — not just bank details; the field list changes, the method does not.

subtitle: Invoice Price Tolerance Testing
intro: Test whether the invoice price tolerance — both percentage and absolute limits — is still appropriate, and confirm it has not been quietly absorbing variances that should have been blocked.

exec_table.directions: Display tolerance limits for invoice verification. Record the tolerance keys, company codes, and both the percentage and absolute columns, plus change history. [Navigation: type OMR6 in the command field, review the tolerance key table, note the change history if available.]
Display table RSEG for your period. Compare invoice value against PO value per line and calculate the variance. [Navigation: type SE16N, enter RSEG, set your date range, execute.]
Sort the variance list by percentage first, then re-sort by absolute value — look for a cluster sitting just under the absolute limit. Count and total them, and check whether the same vendors recur.

Display the blocked invoice list. Do not release anything — this confirms only what the control actually caught. [Navigation: type MRBR in the command field, set your selection criteria, execute in display mode.]

evidence: The OMR6 configuration screenshot (percentage and absolute limits, with change history or a note that none exists), and a variance list sorted by absolute value showing the concentration of invoices sitting just under the absolute limit.
pitfall: A tolerance set wide enough will produce zero blocked invoices by construction — an empty blocked-invoice list is not evidence the control works, it is the reason you need to test the configuration itself.

subtitle: Batch Job Monitoring Testing
intro: Confirm that scheduled batch jobs are actually monitored for failure — not just the backup job — by testing execution history against the expected schedule.

exec_table.directions: Run with job name and user both set to wildcard for your date range, with every status box ticked including Cancelled. [Navigation: type SM37 in the command field, set Job name = *, User name = *, set your date range, tick all status checkboxes, execute.]
Sort the result by status and record the count of cancelled jobs. Open one cancelled job's log to read the failure reason, then open its Step detail to see the program it runs.

Display the job definition to confirm expected scheduling frequency, and compare against what actually appeared in SM37 — a job never released produces no row at all. [Navigation: type SM36 in the command field, locate the job definition.]

evidence: The documented expected execution count written down before running SM37, the SM37 selection screen and result with Cancelled included, one job log and step list, and a schedule-versus-actual comparison showing any missing dates.
pitfall: Leaving Cancelled unticked in SM37 will show zero failures — confidently and wrongly. And "finished" is not the same as "worked": a job that completed having processed zero records still shows as finished.

subtitle: Fixed Asset Depreciation Parameter Testing
intro: Confirm that depreciation is running on the correct parameters — not just running successfully — for assets that transferred in through an acquisition.

exec_table.directions: Check the depreciation run log for your company code and confirm every period shows a completed run. [Navigation: type AFBP in the command field, set company code and period range.]
Display only — record depreciation key, useful life, depreciation start date, and asset class for a sample asset. [Navigation: type AW01N, enter the asset number.]
Display table ANLB for the company code and fiscal year. Group by depreciation key and count usage. [Navigation: type SE16N, enter ANLB, set company code/fiscal year, execute.]
Display the calculation method behind any unfamiliar depreciation key found in ANLB. [Navigation: type AFAMA in the command field, enter the depreciation key.]
Display table ANLA and cross-reference acquisition date/class against the keys found — weight the sample toward acquisitions and transfers. [Navigation: type SE16N, enter ANLA, execute.]

Confirm whether depreciation parameters were later changed and whether that change was approved, using the same technique as Book 26. [Navigation: type SE16N, enter CDHDR/CDPOS for the asset object class.]

evidence: The depreciation run log confirming complete execution for every period, the ANLB extract grouped by depreciation key with any inherited or mismatched keys flagged, and one AW01N Asset Explorer screenshot.
pitfall: Successful execution and correct calculation are two different assertions — a depreciation run can complete every month with no errors while running on parameters that do not match your accounting policy at all, and nothing in the system will flag that a value, rather than a flag, is wrong.

subtitle: Credit Management & Billing-Block Release Testing
intro: Confirm that sales orders blocked for exceeding a customer's credit limit are released only by someone independent of the order's creator, with documented justification on file — not routinely overridden to keep revenue moving.

exec_table.directions: Type VKM4 into the transaction code field at the top-left of the SAP GUI screen and press Enter. Work through the blocked-document worklist and open each document's release history. [Navigation: from the SAP Easy Access menu or command field, enter VKM4, set your date range on the selection screen, and press F8. Double-click a document to see its release status and history.]

Display table VBUK directly to pull your own population rather than relying on VKM4's default worklist filters. [Navigation: type SE16N, enter VBUK, filter on CMGST (credit status) and your date range, execute.]
Display the sales order to confirm who created it. [Navigation: type VA03 (display) in the command field, enter the sales order number, press Enter; check the document header's Created By field.]

Display the customer's credit master data — credit limit, control area, and any recent changes to the limit. [Navigation: type FD33 (or BP for the Business Partner view), enter the customer number, and open the credit management/credit limit view.]

For any release with no documented justification on file, escalate rather than noting it and moving on — a pattern of silent overrides usually means the credit-block control has quietly become theater across more than just the sampled orders.

evidence: The VBUK-based population of credit-blocked orders, the release history and releaser identity per order, the creator-vs-releaser comparison, and a credit-master screenshot for any order where the limit itself may have moved just ahead of the block.
pitfall: A credit block that gets released the same day, every time, by the same person who wrote the order, is not a working control — it's a formality the order has to walk through on its way to happening anyway. Don't stop at confirming the block existed; confirm who broke it, how fast, and on what authority.

subtitle: Billing Cutoff & Revenue Recognition Testing
intro: Confirm that invoices are only created after the corresponding goods have actually shipped — not backdated or pushed through early to hit a quarter-end revenue target.

exec_table.directions: Type VF04 into the transaction code field at the top-left of the SAP GUI screen and press Enter. Review the billing due list for the cutoff window as an orientation step, then verify independently via SE16N. [Navigation: type VF04, set the billing date range on the selection screen, execute.]

Display tables VBRK (billing header) and VBRP (billing items) directly to pull your own population for the last days of the period. [Navigation: type SE16N, enter VBRK, filter FKDAT (billing date) to your cutoff window, execute; repeat for VBRP if line-level detail is needed.]

Display the delivery referenced by each sampled billing document and record the actual goods-issue date and time. [Navigation: type VL03N, enter the delivery number, open the header status or document flow to find the goods-issue timestamp.]
Display the originating sales order for context — requested delivery date, customer, and order value. [Navigation: type VA03, enter the sales order number.]
Any billing document whose creation timestamp precedes its delivery's goods-issue timestamp is a cutoff exception — flag it immediately rather than folding it into a larger sample average.

evidence: The VBRK/VBRP-based billing population for the cutoff window, the goods-issue timestamp from VL03N for each sampled document, and the calculated gap (or violation) between billing and goods-issue timestamps.
pitfall: Comparing dates alone will miss same-day violations — always pull the actual timestamps, not just the calendar date, when testing cutoff at quarter-end.

subtitle: Bank Reconciliation Testing
intro: Confirm that items sitting in the bank clearing account are being investigated and cleared within the policy timeframe, not accumulating as an unmonitored backlog that could mask fraud or error.

exec_table.directions: Type FAGLL03 into the transaction code field at the top-left of the SAP GUI screen and press Enter. Select Open Items and set your key date to period end. [Navigation: enter the bank clearing G/L account, select the Open Items radio button, set the key date, press F8 to execute.]

Review the electronic bank statement post-processing log for sampled aged items to see why they never auto-matched. [Navigation: type FEBAN, select the relevant statement/date, review items still sitting in the exception worklist.]
Display the manual bank statement entry for a sampled item to review its processing history. [Navigation: type FF67, enter the house bank and statement reference, display the entry.]

Display table BNKA (or the house bank configuration view) to confirm every active bank account is included in the reconciliation scope. [Navigation: type SE16N, enter BNKA, execute, cross-check the account list against Treasury's stated reconciliation scope.]
Any account active for transactions but absent from the reconciliation population is a scope gap, not a clean result — escalate before concluding the account has no exceptions.

evidence: The FAGLL03 open-item population for the bank clearing account, the aging calculation, FEBAN processing/investigation notes for the sampled aged items, and the house bank configuration confirming complete account coverage.
pitfall: A bank account excluded from the reconciliation scope produces a clean-looking report by omission, not by being genuinely reconciled — always confirm the population of accounts being tested is complete before trusting an empty exception list. The same completeness check applies to any reconciliation — intercompany, sub-ledger-to-GL, or inventory-to-financial — confirm the reconciling population is complete before trusting a clean result.

subtitle: Tax Configuration Change Testing
intro: Confirm that a change to a tax code's rate was tested, approved, and moved to production on schedule — and quantify what happened to transactions caught in the gap if it wasn't.

exec_table.directions: Type FTXP into the transaction code field at the top-left of the SAP GUI screen and press Enter. Display the tax code and record its current rate and effective structure. [Navigation: enter the country and tax code, press Enter, review the percentage rate fields — display mode only.]
Display table T007A/T007S directly to pull the full tax code list and configured rates independently of FTXP's single-code view. [Navigation: type SE16N, enter T007A, execute.]
Display table BSET for the sample period to see the tax rate actually applied on posted documents. [Navigation: type SE16N, enter BSET, filter by tax code and date range, execute.]

Pull the transport log for the tax code configuration change to establish the exact go-live date and time. [Navigation: type STMS or SE01, search transports referencing the tax code configuration table, note the import date/time to production.]
For every transaction posted between the policy-effective date and the actual go-live date, calculate the dollar impact of the incorrect rate rather than simply noting the gap existed.

evidence: The FTXP/T007A configuration screenshot, the transport history for the tax code, the BSET-based recomputation for the sample, and the dollar-impact calculation for transactions caught between the policy-effective date and the actual go-live date.
pitfall: A tax code showing the correct rate today tells you nothing about what it charged during the window that matters — always confirm the effective date of the current configuration against when it was actually live in production, not when someone claims it was approved.

subtitle: FX Hedge Accounting Effectiveness Testing
intro: Confirm that an FX hedge relationship carries the IFRS 9/ASC 815-required designation memo and effectiveness testing documentation — not just a completed trade with a favorable outcome.

exec_table.directions: Pull the full population of active hedge relationships and their designation dates for the test period.
For each hedge, confirm a designation memo exists dated at or before inception.
Confirm prospective and retrospective effectiveness testing evidence exists for each period.
Trace the hedge's journal entries to confirm the documented accounting treatment was actually applied.

evidence: The Hedge Management Cockpit population export, the designation memo for each sampled hedge with its dated timestamp, the prospective and retrospective effectiveness test results, and the FI posting detail confirming accounting treatment matched documentation.
pitfall: A hedge that is economically effective is not the same as a hedge that is properly documented — IFRS 9 and ASC 815 both require contemporaneous designation and ongoing effectiveness testing, and a retroactively created memo does not satisfy that requirement no matter how effective the hedge actually was.

subtitle: In-House Cash / Intercompany Netting SoD Testing
intro: Confirm that intercompany payments processed through Thornfield's In-House Cash center carry the same segregation-of-duties controls as an external payment run — not a lighter-touch process just because the cash never leaves the group.

exec_table.directions: Pull the population of netting/payment runs for the period, with initiator and approver identified for each.
Display intercompany balance tables for the entities involved to confirm reconciliation.
Cross-check each entity's sub-ledger against the settled amount.
Compare initiator and approver per run exactly as in external payment-run testing.

evidence: The In-House Cash netting run population with initiator and approver per run, the creator-vs-approver comparison, and the intercompany reconciliation confirming settled amounts tie to each entity's sub-ledger.
pitfall: Treating intercompany payments as inherently lower-risk because the cash never leaves the group is exactly the assumption that lets a real segregation-of-duties gap sit unnoticed — the same creator/approver test that applies to an external payment run applies here without modification.

subtitle: Third-Party GRC Tools vs. Native SAP GRC AC
intro: Confirm which platform is authoritative for SoD risk analysis when a client runs both native SAP GRC Access Control and a third-party tool (Fastpath, Pathlock, SailPoint) side by side — and reconcile the difference before trusting either one's exception count.

exec_table.directions: Open the Access Risk Analysis app from the Fiori Launchpad or NWBC, set Analysis Type = User Level, and run for the same scope you'll use on the third-party platform. [Navigation: App Finder search "Access Risk Analysis", set filters, execute, export results.]

Log into the Pathlock Cloud console (or Fastpath / AuditBoard, depending on the client), open Access Risk Analysis, and run the identical scope/period. [Navigation varies by client tenant — request administrator walkthrough on first use.]
Display table USR02 or AGR_USERS to independently confirm the SAP user population both tools should be analyzing. [Navigation: type SE16N, enter the table, execute.]
Request each platform's rule/risk definition export and compare line by line for the risk IDs showing a mismatch. [No SAP GUI navigation — request directly from each platform's administrator.]
Where a mismatch traces to a stale rule mapping or an out-of-scope application, document the root cause explicitly rather than simply reporting the two numbers side by side.

evidence: Risk analysis exports from both platforms for the same scope, the ruleset comparison, the SAP user-master cross-check, and a documented rationale for which platform's output the testing conclusion relies on.
pitfall: Two tools analyzing "the same" access can legitimately disagree — the failure isn't disagreement, it's not noticing it, or trusting whichever number is smaller without checking why.

subtitle: Data Analytics for Full-Population Testing
intro: Recognize when a testing population is large enough that manual sampling risks missing a systemic issue, and use basic data-analytics tooling (SQL, Alteryx, Power BI, ACL) to test the full population instead of a small sample.

exec_table.directions: Display table RSEG for the full test period and export the complete result set — not a pre-filtered subset. [Navigation: type SE16N, enter RSEG, set the date range, execute, then export via the results toolbar.]
Load the exported population and calculate variance-to-absolute-limit for every row in a single pass. [No SAP navigation — this step runs outside SAP GUI, in your analytics tool of choice.]
Build a pivot table or dashboard grouping the full-population result by vendor and sorting by proximity to the tolerance limit. [No SAP navigation — this step runs outside SAP GUI.]

Manually validate a sample of the analytics-identified exceptions directly in SAP before relying on the tool's output. [Navigation: type FB03 or SE16N, pull the specific document identified by the analytics output, confirm it matches.]

If the full-population query surfaces vendors or patterns the original manual sample missed entirely, document that gap explicitly — it says something about the sampling approach, not just about the vendors.

evidence: The full-population extract, the query or formula used to calculate variance, the resulting exception list sorted by threshold proximity, and manual validation of a sample of the analytics-identified exceptions directly in SAP.
pitfall: A manual sample of 25 out of tens of thousands will almost never surface a pattern that only exists in aggregate — when population size and a plausible "stay under the radar" behavior both point the same way, that's the signal to run the full population through a query, not stretch the sample size.

subtitle: GRC 2026 / Joule-Assisted Review & Continuous Controls Monitoring Awareness
intro: Confirm that access-request approvers are still exercising independent judgment when SAP GRC 2026's Joule-assisted recommendations sit next to every request — not simply clicking whatever the AI suggests.

exec_table.directions: Open the Access Request Approval app and review a live pending request to see how the Joule recommendation is displayed alongside it. [Navigation: Fiori Launchpad, App Finder search "Access Request Approval".]
Export the full decision log for the test period, including the AI recommendation field. [Navigation: from the approval app's history view, use the export/download option.]

Pull the elapsed time between request-opened and decision-made for each sampled approval. [Navigation: typically available in the same decision log export, or via SWI1 workflow timestamps if routed through classic workflow.]
Review the change history for any CCM rule Joule generated or modified during the period. [Navigation: open the rule configuration app, select the rule, view its change/version history.]
Treat a near-100% AI-agreement rate as a testing trigger, not a clean result — dig into elapsed time and a sample of the matched decisions before concluding the control operates effectively.

evidence: The approval decision log paired with each Joule recommendation, the match-rate and elapsed-time calculations, and the CCM rule-change approval trail for AI-generated or AI-modified rules.
pitfall: A high AI-agreement rate looks efficient and reads terribly in a workpaper — it's exactly the pattern that should trigger closer testing, not less, since it's indistinguishable from an approver who stopped reading the request and started reading the recommendation instead.

part_title: Manager Track Elective — From Finding to Closure
subtitle: RCM (Risk & Control Matrix) Construction
intro: As engagement manager, translate a walkthrough of the Procure-to-Pay and Record-to-Report cycles into a structured Risk & Control Matrix (RCM) — the document that will define which controls get tested, by whom, and how — before any fieldwork begins.

exec_table.directions: Conduct a structured interview with each control owner, documenting the control exactly as they describe performing it. [No SAP navigation — this is an interview and documentation step.]

Independently confirm the configuration behind any automated control mentioned in the walkthrough. [Navigation: type the relevant transaction (e.g., OMR6, SPRO) in display mode, record the configured values.]
Search the control repository for a prior-cycle version of the control and compare attributes. [Navigation: open the control repository app, search by process area or control name.]
Populate the RCM with each control's full attribute set and testing approach. [No SAP navigation — this is a workpaper-construction step.]
Circulate the draft RCM for control-owner sign-off before scheduling any fieldwork against it.

evidence: Walkthrough notes per control owner, the configuration confirmation for each automated control referenced, the completed RCM with all attributes populated, and control-owner sign-off on the draft RCM.
pitfall: An RCM built entirely from policy documents and never validated against actual system configuration will send testers out to test a control that doesn't operate the way the matrix says it does — as this course's own fieldwork has repeatedly shown.

part_title: Manager Track Elective — From Finding to Closure
shortname: The Control That Was Never Built to Hold
subtitle: Design Effectiveness Testing
intro: Confirm that a control as designed — not yet as operated — is actually capable of preventing or detecting the risk it is assigned to in the RCM, before spending fieldwork hours testing whether it operated.

exec_table.directions: Pull the control's stated objective from the RCM built in Book 36 and restate it as a testable design question.

Display the standard role(s) associated with the control's process and review whether both functions' authorization objects sit in the same role. [Navigation: type PFCG, enter the role name, display mode only, review the Authorizations tab.]
Build a simple who-can-do-what mapping from the role review to visualize where the design does or doesn't enforce separation.
Document the design conclusion explicitly, separate from any operating-effectiveness conclusion drawn from prior fieldwork.

evidence: The RCM's stated control objective, the PFCG role-design review, a RACI-style mapping of who can perform each function, and the design-effectiveness conclusion memo distinguishing design from operating deficiency.
pitfall: Running a full operating-effectiveness sample before confirming design effectiveness can waste an entire testing cycle proving, one instance at a time, something a five-minute role-design review would have shown for the whole population at once.

part_title: Manager Track Elective — From Finding to Closure
subtitle: Operating Effectiveness Sampling
intro: As engagement manager, determine the sample size and selection method for each key control's operating-effectiveness test — matched to the control's frequency and the engagement's reliance strategy — rather than defaulting to the same handful of items every time.

exec_table.directions: Pull the documented frequency for each key control from the RCM built in Book 36.
Apply the standard frequency-based sample-size table and document any deviation with a stated rationale.

Confirm the population source table directly rather than relying on a pre-filtered report. [Navigation: type SE16N, enter the relevant table, confirm record count against any report total being compared.]
Select the sample using the documented method and record the selection rationale in the workpaper.

evidence: The RCM frequency reference for each control, the sample-size determination and rationale, the population-completeness confirmation, and the documented sample-selection method.
pitfall: A sample size that looks rigorous but was drawn from an already-filtered report can be entirely correct in its math and still support the wrong conclusion, because the population itself was wrong before the first item was ever selected.

part_title: Manager Track Elective — From Finding to Closure
shortname: What Kind of Finding Is This
subtitle: Deficiency Classification
intro: As engagement manager, take the findings accumulated across this engagement's fieldwork and classify each one by severity — deficiency, significant deficiency, or material weakness — using a consistent, documented framework rather than gut feel or how uncomfortable the finding is to deliver.

exec_table.directions: Compile every finding from the engagement's fieldwork Books into a single inventory before individually rating any of them.
Recalculate or confirm each finding's full population impact rather than relying on the original sample count.
Check the RCM for a compensating control relevant to each finding before finalizing its severity.
Apply the documented severity framework to every finding and record the specific rationale for each rating.

evidence: The compiled findings inventory, the quantitative impact assessment per finding, the compensating-control cross-reference, and the severity classification memo with documented rationale.
pitfall: Rating every finding the same severity because that's administratively simpler, or downgrading a finding because delivering a "material weakness" conversation is uncomfortable, both break the classification framework's only real job — giving management and the board an honest picture of where the risk actually is.

subtitle: Extensibility Classification, Transport Governance & AI Code Review
intro: As engagement manager, establish the governance checkpoints a control needs to survive Thornfield's move to S/4HANA Cloud under Clean Core — classify the custom object behind the control by extensibility level, confirm every transport touching it carries proper Clean Core sign-off, and review any AI-generated ABAP proposed as its replacement before it ever reaches production.

exec_table.directions: Classify the control's custom object A through D using the Custom Code Migration app output.
Pull the transport log for the object and confirm sign-off and a Clean Core impact note on every entry.
Confirm human sign-off on Clean Core compliance for any AI-assisted ABAP change before it was promoted.
Check the object's documented disposition on the migration worklist against what was actually done.

evidence: The custom-code extensibility classification output, the transport log with sign-off and Clean Core impact notes for the review period, the AI-code review sign-off record where Joule for Developers or an equivalent tool was used, and the custom-code migration worklist cross-reference.
pitfall: Treating 'the report still runs' as proof a control survived Clean Core remediation intact, or treating AI-generated code as pre-approved because it compiled and passed a unit test — both skip the actual governance question, which is whether the object's classification, its transport history, and its review trail can withstand being asked about individually, not just whether the output looks right today.

subtitle: Ghost Employee Testing
intro: Confirm that every active employee record in the payroll master data represents a real, currently employed person — not a duplicate or fabricated identity sharing bank or address details with another "employee."

exec_table.directions: Display Infotype 0009 (Bank Details) across the full population and sort for duplicate account numbers.
Display Infotype 0006 (Address) across the population and sort for duplicate addresses.
Display the individual master record for each flagged match to review employment status.
Confirm with the cost-center manager whether the flagged employee is real and reports to work.

evidence: The Infotype 0009 bank-details extract with duplicate accounts flagged, the Infotype 0006 address extract with duplicates flagged, the individual master record review for each match, and the cost-center manager's confirmation for any unresolved match.
pitfall: A duplicate bank account or address has an innocent explanation more often than not — but closing the finding based on a plausible story instead of an independent confirmation from the cost-center manager is exactly how a real ghost employee stays on the payroll.

subtitle: Unauthorized Pay Rate Change Testing
intro: Confirm that every change to an employee's base pay rate carries a documented, independent approval before it takes effect in the next payroll run.

exec_table.directions: Pull the Infotype 0008 change history for the test period with old/new values, changer, and timestamp.
Display the individual employee's pay infotype history for context on each sampled change.
Confirm each change has independent approval evidence on file.
Review whether the changer's role also permits approval, indicating a design gap.

evidence: The Infotype 0008 change population with old/new values and changer identity, the approval evidence (or absence of it) for each sampled change, the dollar-impact calculation for any unapproved change, and the role review showing whether change and approval authority sit with the same person.
pitfall: An unapproved pay-rate change that turns out to be a reasonable, correctly-calculated raise is still a control failure — the finding is the missing approval, not whether the rate itself was fair. Don't let a defensible outcome soften how the gap gets written up.

subtitle: Off-Cycle / Bonus Payment SoD Testing
intro: Confirm that off-cycle payroll payments — bonuses, corrections, severance — are requested and approved by different people, with the same rigor as a regular payroll run.

exec_table.directions: Pull the off-cycle payroll run population for the test period, including requester and approver.
Compare requester and approver per run.
For a sample, confirm the amount paid matches a documented justification.
Compare off-cycle volume across periods to check for an upward trend.

evidence: The off-cycle payroll run population with requester and approver per run, the requester-vs-approver comparison, the business justification documentation for the sampled payments, and the trend analysis of off-cycle volume over time.
pitfall: Off-cycle payments exist specifically to handle genuine exceptions — the moment they start trending upward as a share of total payroll, that's a sign the exception process has become a routine way to bypass the regular cycle's controls, not evidence the business just has more exceptions than usual.

subtitle: Payroll-to-GL Reconciliation Testing
intro: Confirm that the total payroll processed for the period is fully and accurately reflected in the general ledger — not just that the payroll run itself completed successfully.

exec_table.directions: Pull the payroll posting run summary for the test period.
Pull the GL balances for payroll expense and liability accounts for the same period.
Reconcile payroll posting total to GL balances and identify variance.
Trace any variance to a specific cause and confirm approval on manual adjustments.

evidence: The payroll posting run summary, the GL account balances for the same period, the reconciliation showing any variance, and — for any manual adjustment — the approval documentation for that entry.
pitfall: A payroll run that completes successfully in the payroll system is not the same assertion as "the GL is right" — always independently pull the GL side and reconcile, rather than treating a clean payroll-run status as proof the financial statements reflect it correctly.
